1. The frames show how often buying beat renting, depending on the month someone started. Each small square is a starting month between January 1991 and July 2016. A lit square means the buyer was ahead after ten years. A dark square means the renter was ahead. The sources are FHFA home prices, BLS rents and Freddie Mac mortgage rates. The slide is marked "illustrative", "US only" and "history, not a forecast".

2. Almost nothing changes across the six frames. The grid, colors and labels stay the same. The only real change is that frames 4 to 6 add the caption "2002 to 2007: 6 of 72 (8.3%)". The tan band in the middle of the grid, which seems to match that period, has only a few lit squares. The lit squares are mostly on the left (early 1990s starts), and the dark squares are mostly on the right.

3. It means the answer depended heavily on when you started. Early-1990s starts mostly left the buyer ahead after ten years. For 2002 to 2007 starts, only 6 of 72 months (8.3%) did. Buying did not always win, and it lost badly for starts near the mid-2000s peak. The picture does not show costs such as interest, tax, insurance or repairs separately. It also doesn't say what assumptions sit behind the buyer-versus-renter comparison.

4. I'm giving no advice. The frames show a historical pattern and say it is not a forecast.

5. None.
